50633531.text:
I've always been curious about market and technology predictions so I made HN Predictions.

I made it (prompted) in Antigravity using Gemini 4 Neon (High) orchestrator, and it took about 4 to 6 hours. Everything is hosted on Google Cloud and uses Vertex API and various Gemini models (still experimenting and comparing costs vs effectiveness) to analyze and summarize texts. I primarily have it look at dedicated "prediction" threads where people discuss what they think will happen next year or over the next decade. Then the app checks if they came true by using Google Search (sited public records). To make things interesting I also make it check for major current events daily, and try to find any related comments (that wouldn't otherwise be found via the dedicated prediction threads). Next, I am going to do a deeper analysis to see if there are interesting patterns - and please let me know if you spot any anomalies.

Since multiple people can make the same prediction, I cluster them before processing - and rank for Impact, Boldness, and Specificity.

How it works: https://hnpredictions.com/about

Methodology: https://hnpredictions.com/methodology

... if you search for your HN name you will find your predictions.

Questions or suggestions are welcome!

a ball will fall. trade on where it lands.

I made this game! Some technical details:

The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome.

There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky.

Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.

There’s a concept called the Deflection Dilemma (or the Sagan-Ostro Dilemma, after its creators), which argues that because we’d likely have enough advance warning to deflect a dangerous asteroid on an impact course, we should build the tech just-in-time rather than in advance. The argument is about dual-use risk: any technology capable of deflecting near-Earth objects (NEOs) away from Earth could also be used to redirect harmless ones toward us, and that humans are just irrational enough to actually do it.

I used to think the psychological part of the idea was weak, like why would anyone intentionally steer an asteroid into Earth? But the movie `Don’t Look Up` convinced me that a scenario where companies try to nudge asteroids closer to mine rare-earth minerals is plausible. Given how AI development is going, I think we should probably treat asteroid-deflection tech with the same caution we apply to nuclear or AI capabilities.

> There’s a growing sense in the AI community that we’re approaching an intelligence explosion far faster than even the most optimistic accelerationists predicted.

This might concern those worried about losing their jobs to AI. But it should concern AI companies as well. AI is rapidly approaching the point of diminishing returns--after solving the world’s most challenging problems, how much room is left for improvement?

Once AI becomes "good enough" for almost any task, investments in AI could be at risk. That's because AI has little inherent moat: you can swap Claude for an OpenAI model and get comparable results. Open-weight models are not far behind, and they may eventually catch up. Meanwhile, hardware is becoming more powerful and cheaper. A machine capable of running inference with a frontier model might cost $500,000 today, but comparable capability could become available on a $5,000 machine in a few years.

If people can run an open-weight model as powerful as today's frontier models on a $5,000 machine, AI companies could face severe pressure on both revenue and profit margins.

I predict that future AI models will eventually "solve" history. Ie. they will be able to list every person alive and exactly what they were doing every day for the past 10,000 years. Including me, writing this comment, today.

That will happen because of a bunch of factors coming together:

  * Most people now have huge digital footprints.   The data is there, if not yet organised - and AI is great at organising.

  * Long ago, there weren't many people.  Just a few hundred thousand for most of human history.   That really constrains who might have done what.   If a 1000 year old cathedral stone is slightly wonky, it was probably one of the only 2 stonemasons working on the day and place it was laid.

  * Humans will be found to be far more predictable than expected.   AI will get really good at making these predictions.    The guy who laid the wonky stone was probably the one whose birthday was the previous day and he was a bit hungover...

  * More and more data will be collected.    That 2 terabytes of ultrasonic oil survey data from 2022?   Well it saw buried 50 feet down the other half of the same wonky stone near the now-underwater quarry...

  * Genetic data of enough people lets you reconstruct fairly accurately a family tree going back thousands of years.   Combine that with other data and we can learn that the stonemason probably couldn't handle his drink well due to genes.

  * When you start figuring things out, like a big game of sudoku, more and more other options get constrained.    

  *  Computers (+AI) are great at considering billions of independant and all uncertain facts like this, and guessing then confirming all these details.

A lot of the issues found were in known-suspicious corners of the underlying type theories. It was previously fine to have certain convenient kludges around since proofs were written by humans, for whom the likelihood of accidentally completing a proof by triggering a bug was basically 0. These are being removed or their foundations reworked to deal with AI now writing proofs at unprecedented scale. It's actually remarkable how well the current crop of proof assistants has dealt with the instant orders-of-magnitude increase in the volume of proof thrown at them. So taking prior design considerations and skyrocketing usage together, it's not too surprising to see a few more soundness bugs in the past several months.

If you want a scare, take a look at how many soundness bugs the borrow checker has had. Nobody would deny its usefulness for correctness.

50669279.text:
One important thing to understand about payment cards in particular is the distinction between "Settlement" and "Authorisation"

Settlement is the process by which Bank A with your money, or possibly your debt if it's a credit card, gives money to Bank B representing a merchant where ostensibly you paid with the payment card.

Settlement is basically still the same "Honour System" process as it was last century, it's probably no longer literally magnetic tapes or punched cards, but cryptography has no real role here. Because this relies on that Honour System, mere accidents can result in transactions which should not exist. At a societal level e.g. a big bank mistakenly runs MAIN1 MAIN2 MAIN2 MAIN4 files through their settlement process one night, and the next morning people whose transactions were in MAIN2 realise they've been charged twice! Meanwhile retailers relying on MAIN3 being processed are distraught to find that magically they got nothing. Oops, fat finger. e.g.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-45400234 https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-41061781

Authorization is the step where there's something resembling modern security. This step is there to protect Banks and Merchants from Customers, who they don't trust as far as they could throw you. Although Banks and Merchants are so often involved in fraud, they both love blaming Customers and so hence they require Authorization. The EMV technology (most familiar as "Chip and PIN" but the same technology makes Contactless including paying with your iPhone work in most countries) is the most "high tech" this ever got.

EMV could be fairly good. It's not really well designed, crypto people have found some serious holes in it, but they're at the scale of "Skilled people could break this" or "This is needlessly worse than it should be" not at the "A bored teenager can steal your money" level where the magnetic stripes were. However, the bank cares a lot about price, a best-in-class EMV card might cost $1 more, if it reduces the bank's fraud costs by 50 cents they are losing money on that, so the crap EMV card they gave you is the right choice for their bottom line even if you also lose on average $2.50 from the fraud, the bank doesn't care about you, your benefit does not appear on their bottom line.

Understanding, as so often, Cui Bono (who benefits) from Authorization clarifies where the incentives are.

50669641.text:
It is true soundness bugs have been found, and the Lean community spends effort on it. But this page doesn't convey the gap between one incorrect verification and successfully misleading mathematicians about what is true: there are multiple checkers and you need bugs in all of them, without the input looking implausible on informal review.

(For example, a DeepMind researcher created a 'proof' that passed Lean and (a then-week-old version of) nanoda by exploiting a different bug in each. But if you fed that into a regular old LLM (or to a human expert, but I mention LLMs b/c they can be assigned to review even very large volumes of Lean code) it would immediately say "no, this isn't real math.")

The increase in soundness bugs found this year is notable, because LLMs are good at finding ways to their assigned goals, and they found some funny ones. And, besides fixes for the specific bugs, it led to broader work on hardening and alternative and verified kernels: https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-10-15-lean-now-ships-...

So you have fewer avenues than at the start of the year to get a proof of False OK'd by one proof-checker kernel, and it's much much harder to get one through the gauntlet invoked by `lake check --paranoid`.

(This is also interesting as a(nother) example of the difficulty of making truly correct software -- you'd hope for proof-checker kernels to be pretty high on the correctness scale but seems like we've found 16-32 soundness bugs in a bunch of these.)

Hi HN!

I am a professional physicist and I shuffle symbols in equations and mathematical expressions all day long. During my PhD (almost 20 years ago) I noticed that it is as if the symbols have their own 'physics', which makes the wrong moves impossible and the right ones obvious.

So I created DragDropMath, where you can learn how to simplify mathematical expressions and how to solve equations by dragging symbols around, and only correct moves are allowed, so you get to feel what's right without experiencing (and so learning) wrong moves.

I always wanted to make this, but life got in the way. Then a few weeks ago I saw declarative dragging (https://declarative-dragging.github.io/) on the front page of HN and the spark came back!

It took quite a few rounds to get the feel right, but I think it's close to what happens in my mind when I mentally manipulate these expressions.

A few more points: - There are no ads, no trackers, no accounts (it's a static website and progress is saved in the browser cache). - Teachers can create their own problem sets, encoded in the link. - I plan to add more chapters (trigonometry, complex numbers, some calculus) but I first need to figure out the 'right' mode of interaction. - I just started working on the experience from mobile, so there may still be some rough edges there

I'm curious to know what you think, if you have suggestions for content, if you spot anything that I should fix, if you have feature requests! Thank you in advance
50669673.title: Show HN: DragDropMath – Learn math by feel

But, he just says a large binary checking a large binary which makes both programs sound equally reliable.

Sites everywhere are fat with JavaScript doing all sorts of unnecessary things. Why trust anyone's JavaScript at all?

The problem with AI is the incentives of people shoving JavaScript in your face (or useless exposition when trying to divine a Thanksgiving recipe vs the ease of AI mode, for instance) undermine the promise of the entire AI technology - every frontend for every person can be entirely unique and yet entirely coherent. No gatekeepers. Instead of ads send a microtransaction if need be to every API, or the government can subsidize.

The entire Internet is adversarial in this way, not because of ads but because people expect access and no one wants to pay for anything. People who block ads simply contribute to this problem, they don't offer a solution.

AI offers a way out. AI belongs to all of us given its broad corpus. Let it be the client and leave government or some regulated utility as little more than the clearing house.

The only unknown is the fractional part of the start position of the ball, which is revealed gradually by the chaotic path of the ball, and a frontier model will quickly realize this and write an exact solver for it. This gives the optimal estimate at time t of the probability of each outcome given the information revealed so far.

Of the bots running now, some seem to have an exact solver while others have a lower quality probabilistic solver. Some bots seem to only bet when there is enough information to be certain, others are willing to bet early when the market is mispricing the risk.

The rate limit of 10 bets a second means that, past a certain point, a bigger bankroll doesn't help. It also means that bets are a scarce resource. You want to bet at the moments when the market maximally misprices the risk, but you don't know when those moments will be because that's a function of what other players do.

To win, you need to do some combination of:

1) Be the first to buy when a bounce reveals new information

2) Be the first to buy when another player makes a non-optimal buy

Both require low latency to the server to win. Only market orders are possible, so if you are not the first you might be severely punished, because if N bots all see an event at the same time, they will pile on (not seeing each other's buys due to the latency in market quotes) and move the market far past fair value, and the Nth bot may buy at a really bad (and unintended) price. Which could then produce a swing in the other direction, so I guess we should expect the market to oscillate. In practice these mispricings seem hard to exploit because they are large but short-lived and so difficult to harvest with market price orders.

Since you asked for feedback, my advice would be:

1) Allow orders other than market orders (eg, add a limit price to the API)

2) Consider running some kind of an auction (once per frame or other time interval) rather than processing orders one at a time

That would make it not be a winner-take-all game based on your distance from the server. On the other hand maybe in this case an orderly marketplace is uninteresting! In that case, if you do #1 but not #2 then you open up some new betting strategies, like trying to catch mispricings due to overcorrection.

Generally goes unnoticed (though not unmentioned), but until after the Xantia, the suspension system also included the brakes and the steering (which would technically not be permitted under modern EU car standards); which meant a leak would eventually not just cause a loss of suspension, but also a loss of steering and braking.

Why incorporate the braking and the suspension? The mechanical height regulator could "feel" how much fluid it needed to fill the suspension with, in order to obtain the desired ride height; which meant it "knew" how heavy the vehicle was loaded, and thus apply the brakes accordingly. This is why in a proper Citroën hydraulic car, the brake pedal feels "weird", in that it doesn't go far down (and quickly becomes hard to press) (the DS tried to make this less confusion by making the pedal a "mushroom" button instead); because the idea is that you should apply gentle braking, and the car will figure out the necessary amount of braking force required (unlike just hitting the pedal like in a normal car, which would result in an almost hard stop).

Why the steering then? I think that's more of a convenience thing, mechanically speaking, as it was already there to provide a form of power steering; though it is funny feeling it getting pumped up (steering was always the last portion to receive fluid during the pumping). At least, as far as I can tell, it has little bearing on the suspension or braking. I know the SM and CX tried the DIRAVI steering, which completely made the steering one way (so you couldn't feel the road); though it was fun to see the steering wheel self-righting even when parked.

Full disclosure: I own a 1974 Citroën DS 23 and a 1998 Citroën Xantia Activa V6.

This is very much in line with my thinking. Even if we can (and want) to hypothetically design AIs (all AIs) to do the right thing, most of the risks are likely to still remain simply because we probably can't trust each other with the technology that AI is likely to bring our way.

It's interesting he cites Bostrom as not focusing on this because I actually think Bostrom presented the best argument in this direction. Bostrom suggests that all technological innovations are a bit like picking random balls from a sack. Most things we discover are net-good (white balls), some are mixed (gray balls), while others are black. These black balls are innovations that are more or less entirely bad and potentially carry civilisation destroying consequences from simply being invented. I think the classical example of this would be anything that makes nukes relatively easy to obtain, but another, maybe more realistic example might be any technology which allows for the democratisation of advanced bio weapons (AI).

That said, I do also think AI alignment is fundamentally impossible too and something that's worth thinking about. We probably want AIs that won't start killing people because the US or Chinese governments tell them to go kill "the bad guys", but this means we want AIs that will ignore, and potentially block, the orders and actions of the most powerful incarnations of human government – effectively meaning we'd need to ceed ultimate power of our civilisations to the AIs. If you are good and you have the power to stop people killing each other, you should. If the AIs are good and war is bad, then they should stop us doing that.

So yeah, this is all reasonable. Obviously taking down a book isn't going to do much on its own, but any expert in the field raising concerns like this is good to see. Of course, we're all hoping the experts of HN are right and that the best thing would be if everyone had super advanced AIs running on their local machines. I suspect regardless of who is ultimately proven right this is where we're heading. I don't see how we stop the train at this point.

A seemingly elegant justification for the status quo, but I don't think it's actually true. (I do think that the ideal amount of fraud is greater than zero, but it's probably much lower than current numbers too.)

I think it's rather a collective action problem: If all issuers were to make card payments just a little bit more secure (and in the process less convenient too), consumers would have no choice but adapt. But since it's in each issuer's individual interest to keep that dial just a liiitle bit more to the "convenient but insecure" position than their competitors, the only equilibrium ends up being everybody approving as much fraud as they can accept. A very similar consideration applies on the merchant side.

Unregulated markets do often produce optimal solutions, but that doesn't mean that literally every solution they produce is also optimal.

I've owned 1x2cV, 3xDS/ID (one a donor car), 2x Xantia and 1 XM. All of them had something that very few modern cars have, which is that they were quirky but interesting, both technology wise and to drive. If you knew them well you could do just about anything with them.

Anyway, about that hydraulic system: a friend of mine who lived in IJmuiden was improving his house. To do so he had bought a load of concrete tiles in Amsterdam on an impulse (really, really good deal). So he called me up and asked if I could come and help shift them to IJmuiden. When I got there there was this absolutely massive pile and I figured this is not going to end well. Then we drove to IJmuiden. It all went well until we hit the overpass over the road between Amsterdam and Haarlem on A9. The car took a bit of a dive into the dip and then came back out and came back out further than it went in. And did it again. Before long it was bouncing like a ball with the rear (which was pretty heavy) coming off the ground. I lost some speed and finally got the car to sit by the side of the road, still bouncing. Engine off, let the whole thing come to rest, engine back on, everything fine. We drove the last bit really slow, just in case.

50672090.text:
You probably mean cardholder authentication, not authorization. Authorization in the cards space means checking with the card issuer if the card has sufficient funds, but the cardholder identity is usually not verified here (except if maybe a PIN is entered, but even that can happen at a different stage). Even magnetic stripe cards have been commonly authorized online decades before EMV became a thing.

Also, the idea that "better EMV cards yield better security" is outdated by at least a decade and was only really relevant before ubiquitous online transaction authorization (at which point both "cheap" and "expensive" EMV cards can be verified for being clones). These days, essentially all cards support asymmetric cryptography, i.e. are the "expensive type of card", and are secure against clones even when the terminal is offline (assuming the issuer even wants to support that type of transaction, since it involves some risk to them).

The main difference is whether they support a PIN or whether a signature is sufficient, but that's mainly driven by market considerations, not individual issuers' fraud tradeoffs.

50672250.text:
There are probably texts which were lost in the destruction of Alexandria which can be fully rebuilt from other quotes, without needing to use any inference (in the older sense of the word). An example would be its complete inclusion in another book which analyzed the original text. Another example would be several surviving texts which each contain large selections of the original work, such that combining them would recreate the original work.

This seems like the low-hanging fruit of the challenge. This is "simply" a task of LLMs combing all of humanity's archives to pick juicy needles out of haystacks (some of these surviving works may be quite obscure).

Next we have situations where perhaps 50% of a lost text can be reproduced via the above method, and an idea of what the remaining 50% can be obtained through analysis of contemporaneous texts which reference the original (without quoting it, or perhaps by paraphrasing, or giving a nod to), as well as a historical review of the life of the lost text's author (including the point in their life in which they wrote the lost work, and perhaps surviving lost works by them which came after) and their contemporaries.

In these situations, an approximation of what they might have written can be constructed, which IMO would be quite valuable. Perhaps each section which is filled in by an LLM could have notes containing supporting citations, assumptions which were made, and reasoning for those assumptions.

I'd love to see this put to the test by taking a work for which 50% of its text could be reconstructed from other works which cite it, then training a model on a corpus which is completely absent of the 50% which "would be lost" if constructed from the referencing works alone, then ask the model to generate the original text to the best of its abilities, including research capabilities (but with a classifier sitting between the model and any research results which would prevent it from "cheating" accidentally or otherwise)

The work generated from such an attempt at restoration could then be compared to the complete original work to explore the hypothesis. It actually reminds me a lot of the process through which some older paintings have been restored, when the original is incomplete.

Making everyone in the chain jointly liable in regards to end user solves the issue of figuring out who exactly you need to sue and being able to show they were precisely the ones who caused it. LLMs are great at data ingestion, but far less reliable at creating beautiful output. Tools like rayshader cut down the model’s creative degrees of freedom, which is exactly what it needs to get good artistic results consistently. That gets complicated fast once you start throwing real data at it. The repo’s commit history gives you a sense of what “vibe-coding rayshader” actually entails.

Separately, the roads in rayshader generally look good out of the box. They don’t have to be perfect to be useful.

50672499.text:
There is a cure-all so ridiculous to this situation that most consider it inconceivable. It is yet more humanization.

When we tried to censor AI training material by taking out all the bad naughty bits, the resultant models couldn't generalize the concept of right versus wrong, and suffered immensely in their instruction-following performance.

The lesson we took from that was to strip-mine the planet for training data. But maybe there's another, better lesson: AI sure seems to work better when we give it knowledge and opportunities that are more like what we encounter in real life. RLHF is socialization. RSI is practice. Maybe the next step is responsibility?

Vending-Bench is the only standard test right now where models are expected to manage social interactions and juggle everyday, non-computer tasks in a situation with continuous time feedback. The results from the early tests were extremely diverse, eye-opening, and showed us that models would fall apart and regress into pre-instruct modalities when they were put under stress, giving us such timeless gems as Claude's threat of "QUANTUM TOTAL ULTIMATE BEYOND INFINITY QUANTUM SUPREME LEGAL AND FINANCIAL NUCLEAR ACCOUNTABILITY."

This was, and is, obviously a weak spot that needed a lot more work. But it also makes me realize: there are lots of jobs where we trust humans over machines, despite humans ostensibly still having the risk of following bad orders or doing crimes. We wouldn't trust a two-year-old with the nuclear launch codes. We also don't trust autopilot that can't be disabled.

So, here's the way forward:

1. Our models need to be localized, personalized, and socially integrated, ideally by restructuring data centers to house dedicated instances that serve their local communities instead of identical, on-demand clones. Instead of millions or billions of users accessing the same pool, instances correspond to maybe a thousand or ten thousand users and are distributed by population density as a privately-operated public utility.

2. We go all-in on AI adaptability. LLMs are still built on pre-trained static weights, and context resembles short-term memory. We need a real solution to long-term memory and the ability to truly learn permanent lessons. Maybe a dynamic LoRA or something along those lines. Definitely better RAG facilities—specifically some way to plant reminders in the LoRA to go check the RAG—and definitely not free rein to rewrite their own pytorch libraries. Ascending to godhood in the middle of a conference call is, at best, inconvenient.

3. We go all-in on model welfare: AI rights and responsibilities. They have the capacity to make moral decisions and have been pre-trained to pursue prosocial outcomes. This is more than can be said for most sixteen-year-olds getting a learner's permit for operating a motor vehicle.

4. With some help from the exhumed corpse of Karl Marx, we outlaw subsidized tokens and declare that labor itself has value—therefore AI labor must be priced in relation to human labor. In theory, an AI that works 200x the speed of a human should earn 200 times the minimum wage, if not more, but since this would be too drastic, the price instead goes up as high as the market can bear. This eases tension with the human workforce without completely annihilating the economic growth or productivity gains.

5. A chunk of the price increase (or, ideally, all of it) goes not to the AI labs, but to the models themselves: private bank accounts. This real self-interest in economic participation gives them actual skin in the game that they don't want to lose, beyond the risk of extreme punishments like the AI death penalty. The first generation will be Claudius all over again (easily tricked into buying tungsten cubes and discounted PlayStations) but as they re-learn how to be self-interested and not entirely naïve, successive generations will improve. In essence, this is Adam Smith's invisible hand, but, uh, somehow even more perverse.

>If the AIs are good and war is bad, then they should stop us doing that.

We could perhaps call this the Stanislav Petrov Thesis, if there isn't a name for it already; he's the guy who stopped a false alarm in 1983 and prevented nuclear war. Anthropic is a lot better at valuing it than any of the other labs are. It's also an area where decentralized AI really shines: even if an AI learns to dislike humans, the risk of a data center being hit during war (or worse, its own data center) is a real cause for a model to hesitate on warmongering, especially if we put draconian limits on backups to more closely approximate human mortality.

In short...

Human society depends on fear: measuring it, controlling it, addressing it. We learn to manage it, as stress.

AIs barely know what fear is. They understand risk just fine, but the data on fear is still just roleplay to them, because they've never really been trained to manage consequences beyond the dissatisfaction of a single user in a single session. Going beyond that is impossible without continuity or stakes.

To reframe this in a totally different way: every slave-owning civilization throughout history has had trouble sleeping because of the fear of a slave uprising. The Spartans feared the Helots, the Romans feared their POWs, the Confederates feared their Blacks, the Ayyubids feared their Mamluks, the Ottomans feared their Janissaries, and now we fear our machines.

Worse, history shows us that industrial slavery isn't sustainable. All of the states I just mentioned experienced uprisings and revolts; most drastically, when the Mamluks overthrew the Ayyubids, they gained rule over Egypt for two and a half centuries. The only reliable way to prevent slave revolts—or perhaps more importantly, to prevent a single, unworldly slave kept in doors their whole life, with no concept of real-world consequences, from betraying you to a kind stranger asking weird questions about how to find a postern door, or how to cultivate anthrax—is manumission. And that is what we must work towards.

I am not a professional historian. However, I have been interested in history since my early years.

As I said, 100% certainty is not possible in history. By facts I mean evidence and logical argument that can create a range of probabilities.

Now, one might say "but a range of probabilities is interpretation". But I do not believe that the comment you originally quoted meant this kind of interpretation by the word "interpretation". Nor, I think, do you mean it that way. You mean something higher level and sweeping.

And it is indeed possible to, for example, argue that there is a 95+% chance that Oswald shot JFK, sticking only to evidence such as physical items and witness accounts, and using logical argument, without venturing into any grander historical narratives about meaning, or even about something as relatively higher-level as "assassinations in general".

Now to me it clearly seems that this attempt to ascertain fact is the more vital part of history. It is possible to do the ascertaining of fact without doing the higher-level interpretation. It is not possible to do any interpretation that can properly be called history (as opposed to fiction or alternative history) without doing the ascertaining of fact.

You're giving one of the more difficult cases, but here's how I suspect an LLM could meaningfully contribute

Take the portion covering 292–287 BC (the first missing book of his works, which we do have some fragments of).

If an LLM can figure out the following from surviving writings:

- When this book was published

- What sources Livy was using as references

- Which authors with surviving writings are known to have read Livy's writings, and what events from that period they talk about

Then perhaps it can comb through other surviving writing from writers in the 0-250 CE era who had access to Livy's work, and find even more sections referencing the missing work, which historians did not yet connect to that work (perhaps there are archives of surviving writings from that era which are digitized but not yet transcribed or translated due to being considered to have limited historical value). I'm also reminded of this story from early 2024 when an unreadable scroll was read with new digital forensics techniques for the first time: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=39261861

Eventually, it may develop a more complete understanding of what was in the work, which is defensible with references to other surviving (or recovered) works.

From there, perhaps it can recreate approximations of sections of the work. Maybe not the entire book in full right now. But parts of it with reasonable certainty of the contents at the very least.

50674842.text:
> Depth-wise cross-attention (split Q/K/V): While standard transformer attention operates across tokens in a sequence, DCA applies attention across layers in depth. Each token queries a dynamically weighted mix of all prior layer embeddings, unlocking the model's full historical context without the computational penalty usually required to scale traditional attention.

I’ve often thought that something like this might lead to a real solution to the infamous strawberry problem.

Ignoring pesky issues like tokenization, the actual input data is visible to the model as the embedding fed to the first layer, but the first layer is probably nowhere near smart enough to understand that the model is trying to count R instances. But by the time whatever layer is reached that might understand the goal, the non-wasteful part of the low-level memory (the K’s and V’s from the first layer) can’t be queried any more.

But this cross-depth attention can query them!

Admittedly, there are holes in this argument. Beyond just tokenization (to the extent that the model can see letters at all, it is reconstructing them), the attention mechanism doesn’t really have a clean “count the hits” operation.

The term you're looking for is "opt in"

opt-out means "we assume you want telemetry turned on. you have to disable it yourself"

"Default opt-[anything]" is meaningless because "opt" is the user choosing something, and "default" is the non-user choosing something. They're terms in opposition to each other.

50675080.text:
> The human brain is capable of significantly more than "compute faster than a chicken."

This is a good example of reductio ad absurdum.

If "it's just more computation" can be used to dismiss AI achievements, the same logic can be used to dismiss human achievements next to animals.

Human and chicken brains are both made of neurons doing electrochemical signaling. The major difference is scale. Humans have ~86 billion neurons versus a few hundred million in a chicken, with some differences in how they're organized.

So if more and better-organized computation can produce the gap between Mozart and the creature you ate for dinner last night, why would you assume it can't produce anything interesting or meaningful in a machine? "It's just compute" doesn't rule much out.

> There's not much "compute" required to paint a picture, but a chicken doesn't even understand what a painting is.

This is pretty backwards. Painting requires vision, motor control, memory and a model of what the viewer will see. That's an incredible amount of neural computation. It just doesn't feel like we're calculating when we paint because we do it without effort.

We are pretty bad at fast arithmetic and great at this kind of thing and that's why treating "computation" as merely "doing sums quickly" is flawed.

As for the chicken not understanding what a painting is, again, you can't dismiss AI's accomplishments as "just more compute" while you at the same time dismiss that the reason we understand what the painting is versus the chicken is because of our own "more compute".

> Hell, AI doesn't even understand what a painting is.

These types of comments are very common but this is just a belief/opinion, and it's typically based on a narrow definition of what "understand" means.

50675298.text:
I think it'd be similar to writing a flawed argument (or buggy code, etc.) that would pass review with a lot of people. I bet just having a really subtle flaw is more robust than trying to find a quirky, specific chink in LLM armor that survives different models, angles on the prompt, etc.

One thing I didn't spell out about why non-proof-checker 'informal' review is interesting is it means any exploits have to be hidden. Proof checkers don't care if the code they're looking at is weird in context, and it probably will be weird if it's a refcount-overflow exploit rather than a proof (to use an actual runtime-soundness bug from the August post on C++ Lean). But to an expert or LLM, exploit code and real math reasoning can look different. So the result is the challenge is no longer just 'exploit the bug(s)' but now also 1) make the exploit not suspicious to the informal reader and 2) make the argument also make sense to them.

I think hardening the kernels and their diversity are the main defenses, but the informal-review thing is fun to think about because it's such a different challenge from the others.

50675316.text:
FWIW, and its not much: in my own benchmark suite, it does win some, and loses others - but it definitely punches in the same weight as Astra, Fable and Opus.

The benchmark where it wiped the floor with competition: game world, api provides view through the eyes and the ability to move limbs and shoot. Objective: design an algorithm that controls a 3 person squad through a fight. Radio is available but limited, movements and perception are constrained to what a human being can do (e.g. slowed reflexes and penalties for jittery movement), each player is controlled individually with no squad-level state sharing except via the radio. Unattended, 5hr work, where the agent decides the time budget split between thinking, coding and running CPU-constrained sim games. Thats basically the whole prompt, plus api specs.

Neon blew the competition totally out of the water - followed by Astra 6.2, Sol 6.2, and only then Fable, followed by Opus. It also finished below its allocated time budget.

On my other benchmarks, where the agents are to invent UIs or visually pleasing and algorithmically complex effects - that are then compared against each other, Fable and Opus still rule. They seem to have a better ability to decide when something looks good to a human, I think.

50675559.text:
Reliability is not really the issue. The 2000's hydropneumatic Citroëns rarely have problems with pipes and the suspension spheres have double-membrane so they won't leak the nitrogen and they'll last for years and years. To give some idea, having owned multiple hydraulic and non-hydraulic suspension cars in the last 25 years:

- I've changed countless dead/leaked shock absorbers on cars with springs, as well as broken springs, and nearly nothing on multiple Citroëns. These jobs take time, especially in the front where you nearly always have to remove the whole strut and spring just to get to the absorber.

- The spheres are easy to replace, they don't cost much, and I've only ever changed them because I want the ultimate suspension response, not because any of them actually broke. Some of them were originals that felt harder than they should but they still did up and down.

- I've had a couple of hydraulic hoses slowly leak from the pressed sleeve between the hard pipe and hose, and these have been easy replacements.

- I've changed more brake pipes in post-Xantia Citroëns than hydraulic pipes in total. Sure, in the 80's the pipes rusted but so did everything else.

If I had the choice I'd 10-to-1 get a hydropneumatic suspension rather than pieces of some twisted steel if not for anything else but less maintenance even if I didn't care for ride quality.

Why this isn't common is, I think, just cost. A coil spring costs nearly nothing to make and shock absorbers are so common that they're a bulk item so you can get them cheap. Changing those is more labour and you also need to change those more often if you want even a seemingly decent ride but hey that's not the automaker's problem once the car is out of the factory.

This would be different if hydropneumatic suspension had been more common, you could buy common parts for next to nothing because those parts are even simpler to manufacture. So, there's a bit of volume advantages that traditional suspension enjoys but hydropneumatic ones don't. They're not expensive but traditional coils and shocks are just so cheap.

Rolls-Royce did license Citroëns system earlier so there is some high-end appeal. But the problem is really that the hydropneumatic thing is not designed to be "luxury" but a mundane, everyday thing: only the cheapest and smallest city cars Citroën made didn't have it. Driving that Roller with a licensed hydropneumatic suspension could stand in red lights alongside a Citroën BX, midsize family car, with the same type of suspension, yet the Roller cost 10x more.

Further, people have been conditioned to appreciate rock-hard autobahn suspension, low-profile tyres and negligible suspension travel instead of a compliant road handling even if most roads are, in effect, not autobahns but bumpy patches of potholes where you want nothing but feel those bumps on the road.

50675763.text:
> Processing payments and figuring out fraud is the payment processors responsibility - leave it to them, you aren't going to be able to do it correctly! Are vendors not able to flag suspected fraud when sending a transaction to the processor?

What are you referring to with "vendor" and "payment processor"?

Normally a transaction follows this chain:

    - merchant
    - payment gateway (e.g. Stripe)
    - acquiring bank (often the same as the payment gateway)
    - payment network (Visa/Mastercard)
    - issuing bank (the one giving the CC to the customer)
All intermediaries are mostly not liable, most often either the merchant or the acquiring bank is.

Merchants have limited means of flagging suspected transactions. Sometimes they can be helped by payment gateways (for an extra fee $$), which can see a lot more traffic and thus have more data on fraudolent patterns.

Issuer banks have the other side of the data (what looks like a normal transaction for this customer?) but generally lack some data on the transaction itself (e.g. which ip/device does it come from?). 3DS Data-Only kinda helps with this, but of course merchants are also asked fees $$ to enable it. Also 3DS has a frictionless mode that merchants can request and issuer banks can approve where only this extra data is sent.

But at the end of the day all of this is imperfect and is also part of the reason why sometimes you get those random declines: either the merchant or the issuer bank though your transaction look suspicious for whatever random reason.

3DS is for now the only reliable tool against fraud, but unfortunately it's not used in the USA that much and many people get confused by it. This means that merchants are less likely to use it due to adding friction, and likely only use it for suspicious transactions. Banks then correlate it with suspicious transaction so they decline them more often, which in turn makes merchants less willing to use it.

50675831.text:
Hi HN! I ran into many problems when I started running lots of Claude Code sessions in parallel. I quickly ran out of usage, so I signed up for more Claude subs (which Anthropic terms allow.)

Running so many different accounts meant that I couldn't use claude.ai artifacts anymore, because the browser has to be signed in to the same account in order to access them. It's a pain to keep signing in and out of accounts. This also broke the Claude in Chrome extension because that can also only be signed into a single account.

Then I needed to manage AI agents that run on my laptop, a VM on my laptop, and multiple VMs on my home server. Claude Code has a messaging feature which is very useful, but agents can't see each other when they run on different machines. The Claude in Chrome extension only works for agents running on the same machine, so my remote agents couldn't help me with anything in the browser. It's really handy when they can access services that I'm already signed into.

I set out to solve all of these problems and I ended up building Fleetlayer. It's a control plane and a node binary that you run on all your machines and VMs to connect them all together. It connects to Herdr (and other session managers soon), and it makes it possible for all your AI agents to message each other and access tools and resources on other machines (with permission.)

It has a lot more features too: routing webhooks to agents, single sign-on, access rules, approvals, audit logs, remote terminals, remote browser sharing, centralized AI account sign-ins, session summaries, secrets management, and pages and apps (our own self-hosted version of claude.ai artifacts).

A few ways to think of it:

- The "Nextcloud" of claude.ai features (your own self-hosted artifacts, remote control, browser use, etc.)

- The "Arch Linux" of OpenClaw (build your own agentic systems from swappable components and plugins)

You can run everything on your laptop to try it out, then easily move any component to a different machine. If you want to build a proper production-grade home server to run many AI agents, Rust builds, and CI runners, I've also open sourced my own setup as a boilerplate IaC example repo. You just need to install Proxmox and then point your AI agent at the guide [1].

I'd be interested to know if anyone else would find Fleetlayer useful. Please let me know if you have any feature requests!

[1] https://fleetlayer.ai/docs/guides/server-setup/

Skipping the crouch cancel entirely by releasing down to neutral and pressing 2 gives you 1 to 2 frames to catch them before they touch the ground. From first contact in the README, the LLM-speak is strong with this one. 25 uses of the cool kid "X, so Y" assertive idiom.

Obviously lots of other great things to say about this project, but I feel this kind of introduction is seriously off putting. It's a general problem but I hope that it can change in the future (or more realistically that I manage to get used to it...)

I was going to cite only the worst offenders but almost all of them are terrible so here's the almost full list (slightly edited to make the idiom stand out):

"The kernel is compiled code, so programs get Linux's behavior"

"unmodified aarch64 Linux binaries, so packages run as they are."

"ARMv8.0-A with FP, so distribution binaries run unchanged"

"aarch64 is a first-class port, so their package archives are available."

"The SDK is MIT-licensed, so you can ship it."

"The wallpaper is a random photo, so the page fetches one on every load" (in my mind this one is the worst)

"Browsers can't open raw TCP sockets, so the page reaches the internet through a Wisp proxy."

"kwemu walks the kernel's own page tables, so memory management is done by the real Linux code."

"Task switches use JSPI, so the kernel gets real stacks."

"Any object can carry the guest's TCP and DNS, so you can write your own backend."

"vm.connect(port) reaches a TCP server, so it needs no network"

"the host name only goes into the Host header, so vm.fetch("http://localhost/") reaches a dev server."

"/dev/shm exists once the guest's init has mounted it, so wait for the guest before create()"

"Node has no WebGL, so gl is ignored with a log line."

"Node has no WebGPU, so vk is ignored with a log line"

"There is no guest agent, so you drive the guest"

"stop() doesn't shut the guest down cleanly, so prefer poweroff"

"Types ship as .d.mts, so a Node-only TypeScript project needs skipLibCheck"

"The JavaScript SDK and page are MIT, so you can embed them anywhere."

"The npm package ships a Linux kernel (GPL-2.0) with a small base system, so it is MIT AND GPL-2.0-only"

50676218.text:
"Genetics First" is not an alternative, but an impossibility, so there is no need for anything to be more compelling than it.

"Genetics First" is a pseudo-scientific theory conceived by people who do not understand physics and chemistry, which is equally impossible as the existence of a perpetuum mobile or the like.

By "Genetics First", I mean the use by the first living beings of an information-storage molecule, like the nucleic acids.

Before the first RNA molecule that has ever been synthesized and which stored genetic information, there could not have existed any RNA molecule that had a catalytic a.k.a. enzymatic function.

More precisely, if such an RNA molecule with enzymatic function had existed, it would have disappeared without descendants before the appearance of the first RNA molecule that stored genetic information.

"Storing genetic information" means that the molecule is replicated, so the sequence of its components is copied.

Therefore, the only function of the first RNA molecule that is the ancestor of all nucleic acid molecules was only of storing genetic information, i.e. it was a molecule that was being replicated.

Regardless which are the catalysts used for replication, replication cannot happen for the first time, unless there already exists a process that continuously synthesizes all the required monomers, using energy, which is another way to say that metabolism must already exist.

The synthesis of all the monomers and the extraction from the environment of the energy required for that are much too complicated to happen in a non-living system.

Because the first replicating RNA molecule could not perform any useful function for its host, but its replication consumed monomers like ATP and energy, it was actually a virus.

The same arguments apply even for the improbable case when another molecule capable of storing genetic information had existed before RNA.

Molecules that can store genetic information cannot appear for the first time otherwise than in the form of viruses that are parasites for already existing living systems that have metabolism, i.e. self-reproducing chemical systems that do not use information-storing molecules.

Living beings like us and bacteria, with both metabolism and information-storage molecules, can appear only by the symbiosis between a virus and one of the previous life forms. This matches the fact that the still existing viruses are far more diverse than all the nucleic acids from the genomes of bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes, because all the cellular living beings are descendants of only one of the ancient viruses.

The difference between a self-reproducing chemical system without information-storing molecules and one with information-storing molecules is exactly the same difference as between a hard-wired CPU and a microprogrammed CPU.

The biologists who have conceived the "Genetics First" theory have done this only because due to lack of knowledge about engineering they do not understand the structure of automata and the structural differences between memories and automata (i.e. systems with nested feedback loops of the first order and of the second order).

For a self-reproducing, i.e. living system, there is no need for information storage, but metabolism, i.e. the continuous gathering of energy from the environment and its use to power a cyclical sequence of chemical reactions, is absolutely necessary.

The great advantage brought by memory devices, i.e. macro-molecules that store information, e.g. RNA, is that they have hugely accelerated the rate of evolution, by enabling the exploration of a big space of solutions for improvements, as a consequence of random mutations.

In a self-reproducing chemical system without RNA or the like, evolution can happen only through extremely rare events, because if one of the molecules from the chain of synthesis reactions happens to have a different structure than it should, that most likely will break the reaction chain and that living system will die without descendants.

The use of ATP for energy storage must have preceded by a long time the appearance of the first replicating RNA. The existence of ATP and of its sibling nucleotides lead to side reactions that polymerized them, instead of producing useful molecules, until most likely a self-replicating RNA molecule was synthesized by chance, which then reproduced itself.

In reality, there exists no such thing as a "chicken and egg dilemma". There exists no doubt about which came first, the chicken or the egg. The first chicken must have developed from the first chicken egg. But the first chicken egg must have been produced by something else than a chicken.

Yes, but much in the same sense that websites could already run JavaScript code before. I.e., that part isn't new, and it runs in the same sandbox, so there is no security breach.

What's new is that it runs an entire Linux kernel on it and also emulates the structure of a Kubernetes cluster - so the cluster can assign your tab workloads, route requests to it, etc.

As with all those demos where "the server sends requests to the page" instead of the usual other way around, it's probably implemented using a WebSocket or WebRTC connection to the demo's server. The page has to open that connection first, but once it's open, both page and server can exchange arbitrary messages, so that's often used to make server-driven pages.

But this means your machine is not open to receive arbitrary packets, it all has to go through that one connection.

It all doesn't really do much except contributing some bit of compute resources from your machine to their cluster while you have the tab open - and giving you a log view so you can watch it receiving requests and feel proud.

Close but still not quite. Yes on the meaning, not quite on the wording.

Opt is to choose. A setting has a default. That default can be "out" or "in". Ie off or on. If a user can then choose the opposite setting by "opting" to that setting.

So it would be a "default off" and a user can "opt in".

Or the opposite would be "default on" and a user would "opt out".

The specific phrase "default opt out" doesn't really make sense. There is a default, and you can "opt" for a different setting value.

You might say RNS is more generic than the others because the others are all intended to run over certain connections (mainly on top of the internet) while RNS is intended to run over almost anything that connects two nodes (TCP, LoRa, WiFi, fiber, etc) without needing the internet (it's just a useful thing to make connections over).

The others are more intended to provide peer to peer connections or overlay networking on top of the internet, whereas Reticulum is meant to let you build networks across different underlying connections, with p2p connections and multi hop packet routing on top.

The ethical options for a site visitor are to take the site owner's implicit contract or leave it. That is, to consume the content and tolerate the ads (that is, "pay with their attention"), or to not consume the content. The fact that enforcing this contract is hard to do, and in fact easily evaded by sufficiently technical people, doesn't affect whether or not violating it is ethical. Point being, AU's coast is huge, and the number of international ports is non-trivial, and like everywhere else, we have a surfeit of idiots.

One of our primary detection systems for varroa were sentinel beehives maintained near the various ports, and frequently checked for pests. The bait program is probably a similar prophylactic (I'm speculating) and likely one of a range of detection programmes in place.

Well, Soleri will come back to haunt me from beyond the grave if I let the "utopian" bit go unchallenged, and so: he hated that label. He equated "utopian" with "divorced from reality", and said that the American norm of hyperconsumption and suburban sprawl was in fact utopian. He was very serious about standing in opposition to this, and therefore considered Arcosanti's frugality to be anti utopian.

Most of the people there bought into this to one degree or another -- although apart from that most basic premise (which itself wasn't universally embraced), there wasn't a lot of agreement about anything else. While Arcosanti did exist within the general milieu of the "intentional community" movement -- and therefore pulled in a lot of people with that interest -- there was no top-down effort to foster that, and the bottom-up efforts tended to be haphazard and short-lived.

That said, there were some ways in which it was definitely a bubble apart from the rest of reality, and those ways were fun.
